## What it is

Many changes can push an outcome either way. An intervention can help some people and hurt others. A behavioral nudge can raise or lower participation. A policy can increase or decrease a risk. The one-way street fallacy is reasoning as if the change could only go in the direction you happen to be thinking about: "this can only help," *the worst case is no effect.*

## Why it matters

The fallacy hides costs and risks. Interventions get promoted as "can't hurt, might help," and analyses count only the people who benefited. Effects with mixed signs get summarized by their positive part. Statistically, it is like running a one-sided test or using a one-sided prior without justification. You never look for the effect that goes the other way, so you never find it.

## How it works

Let individual effects be $\tau_i \sim \mathrm{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$. A one-way accounting reports something like "the share helped," $\Pr(\tau_i > 0)$, or the average among those helped, $\mathrm{E}[\tau_i \mid \tau_i > 0]$. Both are positive *whatever* the value of $\mu$. Even when $\mu < 0$, so that the policy hurts on average, the one-way summary sounds like good news. The two-way accounting reports $\mu$ along with both tails.

## Simulated example

A policy has heterogeneous effects across 5,000 people. The one-way analyst counts who was helped and by how much. The two-way analyst also counts who was hurt.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {rng, range, mean, fmt, pct} from "../js/stats.js"
```

```{ojs}
viewof mu = Inputs.range([-1, 1], {value: -0.2, step: 0.05, label: "Average effect μ"})
viewof sigma = Inputs.range([0.1, 2], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "Spread of individual effects σ"})
viewof seed = Inputs.range([1, 500], {value: 45, step: 1, label: "Random seed"})
```

```{ojs}
street = {
  const r = rng(seed);
  return range(5000).map(() => ({tau: r.normal(mu, sigma)}));
}
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  ariaLabel: "The One-Way Street Fallacy: simulation chart",
  ariaDescription: "Horizontal axis: Individual effect of the policy. Vertical axis: People. The chart updates with the controls above it, and the summary below the charts states the result in words.",
  height: 260,
  x: {label: "Individual effect of the policy", grid: true},
  y: {label: "People"},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectY(street, Plot.binX({y: "count"}, {x: "tau", fill: d => d.tau > 0 ? "#2166ac" : "#d6604d", thresholds: 50})),
    Plot.ruleX([0], {stroke: "currentColor"}),
    Plot.ruleX([mu], {stroke: "currentColor", strokeDasharray: "4 3"}),
    Plot.ruleY([0])
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const helped = street.filter(d => d.tau > 0), hurt = street.filter(d => d.tau <= 0);
  return html`<div class="sim-readout">${md`One-way summary: "The policy helped **${pct(helped.length / street.length)}** of people, by an average of **${fmt(mean(helped.map(d => d.tau)))}**." Two-way summary: it also hurt **${pct(hurt.length / street.length)}**, by an average of **${fmt(mean(hurt.map(d => d.tau)))}**, and the net average effect is **${fmt(mean(street.map(d => d.tau)))}**. Same data, opposite impressions.`}</div>`;
}
```

## Key takeaways

::: takeaways
- Most interventions can push in both directions. Look for both.
- "Share helped" and "average gain among the helped" are positive by construction. Report net effects and the harms.
- Use one-sided tests and priors only when you have a real reason to rule out the other direction.
:::
